edges.title: A Javanese gamelan in Paris reshapes Debussy’s ear

works.from: Javanese gamelan at the Exposition Universelle, Paris (1889)

edges.claim: [[debussy]] heard a Javanese gamelan at the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1889, and its scales, melodies, rhythms and layered textures appealed to him. Their echoes are heard in Pagodes, the first piece of the piano suite Estampes, which uses pentatonic scales and mimics gamelan melodies. He later wrote that Javanese music “obeys laws of counterpoint which make Palestrina seem like child’s play”.

sources.title: Brent Hugh: Claude Debussy and the Javanese Gamelan

edges.title: Mallarmé’s faun finds its music
edges.claim: [[debussy]]’s orchestral prelude, first performed in Paris on 22 December 1894 under Gustave Doret, takes Mallarmé’s poem as its subject; Debussy called it “a very free illustration” of the poem, not a synthesis of it. Mallarmé had doubted that music should be set beside poetry, but after attending the premiere at Debussy’s invitation he wrote that the music went further than his text “into nostalgia and into light”.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune

edges.title: Hokusai’s wave on the cover of La mer

works.to: La mer, first edition of the orchestral score (Durand, 1905)

edges.claim: The first edition of the orchestral score of La mer (Durand, 1905) carried a detail of Hokusai’s Great Wave off Kanagawa on its cover: roughly the left half of the print, the great wave with a smaller wave in front of it. The choice of the print is credited to [[debussy]] and is read as a sign of how much Japanese art meant to him. What is documented is the cover; how far the picture shaped the music is a matter of interpretation.

sources.title: Eastman School of Music, Sibley Library: Claude Debussy, La Mer

art.file: File:Debussy - La Mer - The great wave of Kanaga from Hokusai.jpg
art.caption: Cover of the first edition of Debussy’s La mer (Durand, 1905), with a detail of Hokusai’s Great Wave.

edges.title: Debussy mocks Tristan in a cakewalk
edges.claim: In Golliwogg’s Cakewalk, Debussy alludes satirically to [[wagner]]’s Tristan und Isolde: the opening bars turn the Tristan chord into a jaunty, syncopated arpeggio, and the middle section is interrupted several times by a Tristan phrase marked avec une grande émotion. Debussy had heard the first act of Tristan at the Concerts Lamoureux in 1887 and judged it “decidedly the finest thing I know”, so the joke is aimed at a work he knew well.

edges.title: Debussy orchestrates two Gymnopédies

works.from: Debussy’s orchestration of Gymnopédies Nos. 3 and 1 (1897)

edges.claim: In February 1897, when Satie’s popularity was waning and his finances deteriorating, [[debussy]] orchestrated the third and first Gymnopédies to draw public attention to his friend’s music. When Debussy published the scores two years later he reversed the numbering, so that Satie’s first became his third. The two had met in 1890 and found each other kindred spirits in their experimental approach to composition.

edges.title: Péladan makes Satie composer to the Rose+Croix

works.from: Salon de la Rose+Croix, Paris (10 March–10 April 1892)

edges.claim: Sâr Joséphin Péladan, founder of the Ordre de la Rose-Croix Catholique, invited [[satie]] to become the order’s official composer. For Péladan’s first Salon de la Rose-Croix (10 March–10 April 1892), each gathering opened with a Solemn Mass of the Holy Ghost, preceded by three fanfares for harp and trumpet that Satie composed. They were published as Sonneries de la Rose+Croix, music written for the order’s ceremonies rather than the concert hall.

sources.title: Interlude: Erik Satie, The Rosicrucian Adventure

edges.title: Strauss answers Nietzsche in a tone poem
edges.claim: [[richard-strauss]] conducted the first performance of his tone poem in Frankfurt on 27 November 1896, and named its sections after chapters of Nietzsche’s book (“Of the Backworldsmen”, “Of the Great Longing”). Strauss insisted that he had not meant to write philosophical music or to portray Nietzsche’s work, but “to convey in music an idea of the evolution of the human race” up to Nietzsche’s idea of the Übermensch.

sources.title: Rhode Island Philharmonic: The story behind Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra
Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra: program notes, Also sprach Zarathustra

edges.title: Strauss ends Metamorphosen on Beethoven’s funeral march
edges.claim: At the end of Metamorphosen, [[richard-strauss]] quotes the first four bars of the Marcia funebre from [[beethoven]]’s Eroica Symphony and writes beneath them “IN MEMORIAM!”. A direct quotation from bar 3 of the march also appears earlier in the score as one of the work’s themes, so the funeral march is present throughout the piece before it is named at the close.

edges.title: A rune singer teaches Sibelius how Finnish sings
edges.claim: At the end of 1891 [[sibelius]] travelled with the aesthetician Yrjö Hirn to Porvoo to hear the Izhorian rune singer Larin Paraske. Sibelius recalled that he mainly noticed how a rune singer uses Finnish, prolonging and stressing the last syllables of words, and that he did not yet realise how famous she was. Kullervo, whose vocal movements set runos of the Kalevala, followed in 1892.
edges.note: Hirn’s recollection and Sibelius’s own account place a hearing at Porvoo at the end of 1891, while Sibelius later claimed he first met Paraske on his 1892 honeymoon in Lieksa. That he heard her is documented; where and when he first did is not settled, and how far her singing shaped Kullervo is interpretation.

sources.title: Finnish Music Quarterly: “Utterly Finnish, peculiarly original”
sources.locator: Hirn’s account of the 1891 Porvoo trip

edges.title: Scriabin’s 24 Preludes follow Chopin’s plan
edges.claim: [[scriabin]]’s Op. 11 keeps strictly to the circle of fifths to cover every major and minor key, the plan of [[chopin]]’s Op. 28 set. Both cycles are built alike, with pieces arranged in relative major and minor pairs, and the resemblance sits beside a wider spiritual kinship with Chopin that runs through Scriabin’s early music.
edges.note: The sources describe the likeness of construction between the two cycles; a statement by Scriabin that he modelled Op. 11 on Op. 28 was not found.

edges.title: Tolstoy’s Kreutzer Sonata becomes a string quartet
edges.claim: [[janacek]] wrote his First String Quartet between 13 and 28 October 1923, inspired by Tolstoy’s novella The Kreutzer Sonata, which had itself been inspired by [[beethoven]]’s violin sonata of that name. He had used the novella once before, in a Piano Trio of 1908–09 that is lost; surviving fragments suggest similarities to the quartet. The Czech Quartet gave the first performance in Prague on 17 October 1924.

edges.title: Elgar sets Newman’s poem of a dying soul
edges.claim: [[elgar]] had owned a copy of Newman’s poem since at least 1885, and in 1889 he was given another as a wedding present; that copy carried handwritten transcriptions of notes made by General Gordon. He thought of the text in musical terms for years before setting it for the Birmingham Triennial Festival, where The Dream of Gerontius was first performed on 3 October 1900.

edges.title: Nimrod hints at Beethoven’s Pathétique slow movement
edges.claim: Elgar said Nimrod came from a day when he was ready to give up composing and his publisher August Jaeger urged him on, pointing to [[beethoven]], who wrote more and more beautiful music despite his worries, and singing the theme of the Pathétique sonata’s slow movement. Elgar told Dora Penny that the opening bars of Nimrod were made to suggest that theme: “Only a hint, not a quotation”.

edges.title: Puccini walks to Pisa to hear Aida

works.to: Puccini’s career in the opera house

edges.claim: In 1876, aged eighteen, [[puccini]] walked about twenty kilometres from Lucca to Pisa to hear the first local performance of [[verdi]]’s Aida. He said later that when he heard it in Pisa he felt “a musical window had opened for me”, and the experience is credited with turning him from church music towards the theatre.

sources.title: Choirs.org.uk: Puccini, Messa di Gloria, programme notes

edges.title: A Chinese music box gives Turandot its tunes

works.from: Chinese melodies on a music box owned by Baron Fassini-Camossi

edges.claim: Baron Edoardo Fassini-Camossi, a former Italian diplomat in China, gave [[puccini]] a music box that played four Chinese melodies. Puccini worked three of them into Turandot, the most memorable being the folk melody “Mòlìhuā” (“Jasmine Flower”), which serves as a leitmotif for the princess’s splendour. In all, eight of the opera’s themes appear to be based on traditional Chinese music.

edges.title: George’s poems bring a voice into the quartet

works.from: Stefan George, Litanei and Entrückung (Der siebente Ring)
works.to: String Quartet No. 2, Op. 10, movements III–IV (1908)

edges.claim: In the last two movements of his Second String Quartet, [[schoenberg]] set poems by Stefan George for soprano, adding a voice to a genre that had never had one. The Rosé Quartet and the soprano Marie Gutheil-Schoder gave the first performance, and a critic of 1914 called the innovation Beethovenian, alluding to the choral finale of the Ninth Symphony.

edges.title: Schoenberg dedicates Harmonielehre to Mahler’s memory

works.from: Gustav Mahler, who died in May 1911

edges.claim: [[schoenberg]] wrote his Harmonielehre in the summer of 1910 and published it in 1911 with the dedication “Dem Andenken Gustav Mahlers ist dieses Buch geweiht” (“This book is dedicated to the memory of Gustav Mahler”). [[mahler]] died on 18 May 1911, and the dedication makes the book Schoenberg’s memorial to him.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Arnold Schoenberg and his relation to Gustav Mahler

edges.title: Kandinsky draws Schoenberg into the Blaue Reiter

works.from: Kandinsky’s letters to Schoenberg, from 18 January 1911
works.to: Schoenberg’s contributions to the Blaue Reiter exhibition and almanac (1911–12)

edges.claim: After hearing [[schoenberg]]’s music at a Munich concert on 2 January 1911, Kandinsky wrote to him on 18 January: “In your works, you have realized what I, albeit in uncertain form, have so greatly longed for in music.” Schoenberg visited Kandinsky, Gabriele Münter and Franz Marc in Murnau, and the painters planned an exhibition and an almanac that drew in artists of every medium. The two corresponded until the First World War broke contact in 1914.

sources.title: Sarah Tanner, thesis on Kandinsky and Schoenberg (Auburn University at Montgomery digital archives)
sources.locator: the concert of 2 January 1911 and the letter of 18 January

edges.title: A Schoenberg concert becomes Impression III

works.from: Concert of Schoenberg’s music, Munich (2 January 1911)

edges.claim: Kandinsky’s painting Impression III (Concert) was inspired by a concert of [[schoenberg]]’s works in Munich on 2 January 1911, which Kandinsky attended. He was so enthralled by the music that he wrote to Schoenberg within days, beginning an exchange of letters that lasted until 1914.

sources.title: Sarah Tanner, thesis on Kandinsky and Schoenberg (Auburn University at Montgomery digital archives)

art.file: File:Wassily Kandinsky - Impression III (Concert) - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: Kandinsky, Impression III (Concert), 1911, painted after hearing Schoenberg’s music in Munich.

edges.title: Berg begins seven years of lessons with Schoenberg

works.to: Berg’s early works, from the Piano Sonata, Op. 1

edges.claim: Berg studied counterpoint, music theory and harmony with [[schoenberg]] between 1904 and 1911. He adopted his teacher’s principle of developing variation and, later, the twelve-tone technique, which shapes the Lyric Suite and the Violin Concerto.

edges.title: Berg sees Woyzeck on stage and begins an opera
edges.claim: In May 1914 [[berg]] attended a performance in Vienna of Büchner’s play, left unfinished at the author’s death in 1837, and was moved to set it. The opera that followed, Wozzeck, kept the play’s fragmentary scenes in order and was completed after the First World War.

edges.title: Berg ends the Violin Concerto on Bach’s chorale

works.from: Cantata BWV 60, closing chorale “Es ist genug”

edges.claim: Berg wrote his Violin Concerto “to the memory of an angel” after the death of Manon Gropius, and built its last section on the chorale “Es ist genug” from [[bach]]’s cantata O Ewigkeit, du Donnerwort. The last four notes of Berg’s tone row, rising by whole tones, are also the first four notes of the chorale, and in the score a footnote explains the marking CH as the chorale motif. Berg sets the tune a semitone above Bach’s A major, the solo violin giving the first phrase before the clarinets state Bach’s harmonisation.

sources.title: IMSLP: Violin Concerto (Berg), Universal Edition score, 1936

edges.title: Berg hides Tristan inside the Lyric Suite
edges.claim: The last movement of [[berg]]’s Lyric Suite develops the Tristan motif along with the rest of its material, by Berg’s own analysis, through strict adherence to the twelve-note series. In January 1977 George Perle was shown a copy of the first printed score annotated in red, blue and green by Berg, which revealed a secret programme about Berg’s love for Hanna Fuchs-Robettin; the suite was publicly dedicated to Zemlinsky, whose Lyric Symphony it also quotes.

sources.title: The Cambridge Companion to Berg: Secret programmes (chapter 8)

edges.title: Webern re-scores Bach’s six-part Ricercar
edges.claim: Between December 1934 and early 1935 [[webern]] orchestrated the six-voice ricercar from [[bach]]’s Musical Offering for a chamber orchestra of single winds, harp, timpani and strings. The first performance was in London on 25 April 1935. Webern keeps Bach’s notes and divides the lines among the instruments, so that melodies pass between colours: the principle he called Klangfarbenmelodie.

sources.title: Universal Edition: Bach/Webern, Fuga (2. Ricercata) a 6 voci

edges.title: Webern edits Isaac and learns the interplay of parts

works.to: Webern’s doctoral edition and his later counterpoint

edges.claim: For his musicology doctorate under Guido Adler, [[webern]] edited the second part of Heinrich Isaac’s Choralis Constantinus. As a composer he would emulate its “subtle organization in the interplay of parts”, a discipline he carried from the study of Renaissance polyphony into his own writing.

edges.title: Bartók records peasant songs on the phonograph

works.from: Peasant songs recorded in Békés County and elsewhere (1906–08)
works.to: Bartók’s folk-song collections and the music built on them

edges.claim: [[bartok]]’s first year of substantial folk-song collecting was 1906: that summer he used a phonograph on his first systematic trip, to Békés County, and over the year he collected more than a thousand Hungarian songs and some three hundred Slovak ones. In 1907–08 he went on to Felsőireg and to the Transylvanian regions of Csík and Gyergyó. Following Béla Vikár, he used the phonograph from the beginning to complete his written notes with sound recordings.

sources.title: Institute for Musicology, Budapest: Béla Bartók’s significance in Hungarian folk music research

edges.title: Kodály brings Debussy’s scores to Bartók

works.from: Debussy’s scores, brought from Paris by Kodály

edges.claim: Beginning in 1907 [[bartok]] came under the influence of [[debussy]], whose compositions his friend Kodály had brought back from Paris. The discovery came as Bartók was already absorbed in collecting peasant music, so French harmony and Hungarian folk material reach his work together.

edges.title: Stravinsky studies with Rimsky-Korsakov until 1908
edges.claim: While studying law at the University of Saint Petersburg, [[stravinsky]] met [[rimsky-korsakov]] and studied music under him until the older composer’s death in 1908. Soon afterwards Stravinsky met Sergei Diaghilev, who commissioned the ballets for the Ballets Russes that made his name.

edges.title: The Rite’s opening bassoon sings a Lithuanian tune

works.to: The Rite of Spring, opening bassoon solo (1913)

edges.claim: [[stravinsky]] acknowledged that the opening bassoon melody of The Rite of Spring was derived from an anthology of Lithuanian folk songs, but maintained that this was his only borrowing from such sources. Later scholars have identified several more melodies in Part I that came from the same Lithuanian collection, and Richard Taruskin’s study of the sketches traced further Russian folk sources.

sources.title: The Orchestral Bassoon: Stravinsky, The Rite of Spring
sources.locator: opening solo; notes citing Taruskin, “Russian Folk Melodies in The Rite of Spring” (JAMS, 1980)

edges.title: Stravinsky recomposes music then thought to be Pergolesi’s
edges.claim: Pulcinella, first danced in Paris in May 1920 with designs by Picasso, is a ballet on a commedia dell’arte libretto and music then believed to be by Pergolesi. The attribution has since been shown to be spurious: some of the music may be by Domenico Gallo, Unico Wilhelm van Wassenaer, Carlo Ignazio Monza and Alessandro Parisotti. [[stravinsky]]’s score recomposes it, so the influence is of an eighteenth-century idiom rather than of Pergolesi himself.

edges.title: Stravinsky hears Pierrot lunaire in Berlin
edges.claim: In the winter of 1912 [[stravinsky]] was in Berlin for performances of his ballets by the Ballets Russes, and attended a performance of [[schoenberg]]’s Pierrot lunaire, conducted by the composer, less than two months after its premiere. He had already composed the first of his Three Japanese Lyrics as a song with piano, but after hearing Pierrot he decided to give the songs a somewhat similar coat of instrumental colour.

sources.title: Hollywood Bowl: Stravinsky, Three Japanese Lyrics

edges.title: Hymn tunes and town bands become Ives’s material

works.from: Hymn tunes, town-band music, Stephen Foster

edges.claim: The sources of [[ives]]’s tonal imagery included hymn tunes and traditional songs. He also incorporated the melodies of town bands at holiday parades, fiddlers at Saturday-night dances, patriotic songs, sentimental parlour ballads and the tunes of Stephen Foster.

edges.title: Beethoven’s Fifth motif runs through the Concord Sonata
edges.claim: The opening bars of [[beethoven]]’s Fifth Symphony are quoted in each movement of [[ives]]’s Concord Sonata, whose four movements portray Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts and Thoreau. Ives drew on material dating back to 1904, began substantial work around 1909 and largely completed the sonata by 1915; it was first published in 1920.

edges.title: Leipzig’s Bach competition prompts Shostakovich’s 24 Preludes and Fugues
edges.claim: In 1950 [[shostakovich]] sat on the jury of the first International Johann Sebastian Bach Competition at Leipzig, held for the bicentenary of [[bach]]’s death. The young Tatiana Nikolayeva from Moscow, who had come prepared to play any of the 48 preludes and fugues on request, won the gold medal. Inspired by the competition and her playing, he returned to Moscow and began his own cycle of 24 preludes and fugues, which Nikolayeva premiered in Leningrad on 23 December 1952.

edges.title: Sollertinsky teaches Shostakovich to love Mahler

works.from: Mahler’s symphonies, introduced by Ivan Sollertinsky

edges.claim: [[shostakovich]]’s close friendship with the musicologist and theatre critic Ivan Sollertinsky began in 1927. Shostakovich later said that Sollertinsky “taught [him] to understand and love such great masters as Brahms, Mahler, and Bruckner”. Mahler’s music left a lasting mark on his style, which combines the grotesque with ambivalent tonality.

edges.title: Shostakovich tells Gubaidulina to continue her “mistaken” way

works.from: Shostakovich’s verdict on a Conservatoire examination
works.to: Gubaidulina’s early music at the Moscow Conservatory

edges.claim: [[gubaidulina]]’s music was judged “irresponsible” during her studies at the Moscow Conservatory because it explored alternative tunings. When [[shostakovich]] evaluated one of her examinations he encouraged her to continue on her path, although others, among them Tikhon Khrennikov, called it “mistaken”. She went on to the breakthrough of her violin concerto Offertorium in 1980.

edges.title: Gubaidulina scores Bach’s royal theme in Webern’s manner

works.from: Musical Offering, BWV 1079: the royal theme (1747)

edges.claim: Offertorium is centred on the theme that Frederick the Great gave to [[bach]], the basis of the Musical Offering. [[gubaidulina]] orchestrates the theme with a Klangfarbenmelodie technique reminiscent of Webern, passing it around different instruments to exploit their timbres. The piece was her first major breakthrough.

edges.title: Shostakovich dedicates his Fourteenth Symphony to Britten
edges.claim: [[shostakovich]] dedicated his Fourteenth Symphony, a song cycle on poems about death, to his close friend [[britten]], who conducted its Western premiere at the 1970 Aldeburgh Festival.

edges.title: Britten builds his Young Person’s Guide on Purcell

works.to: The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, Op. 34 (1945)

edges.claim: [[britten]]’s Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, subtitled Variations and Fugue on a Theme of Purcell, is based on the second movement, a rondeau, of Purcell’s Abdelazer suite. It was commissioned for the British educational documentary film Instruments of the Orchestra, released on 29 November 1946.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra

edges.title: Auden writes Britten’s first music drama
edges.claim: [[britten]]’s first music drama, the operetta Paul Bunyan (1941), has a libretto by W. H. Auden. The partnership had begun earlier, in the small group of regular contributors to the GPO Film Unit that Britten joined in the 1930s, where Auden was another of the writers.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Benjamin Britten
sources.locator: GPO Film Unit; America and Paul Bunyan

edges.title: Colin McPhee’s Balinese transcriptions reach Britten

works.from: McPhee’s piano-duo transcriptions of Balinese gamelan

edges.claim: While in the United States, [[britten]] first encountered Balinese gamelan music through transcriptions for piano duo by the Canadian composer Colin McPhee, who had lived in Bali from 1931 to 1938. The two met in the summer of 1939 and performed some of the transcriptions for a recording. Britten later built many gamelan elements into the ballet The Prince of the Pagodas, including a simulation of the seven-tone pelog tuning on Western instruments.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Prince of the Pagodas
sources.locator: Influence of Balinese gamelan on the music

edges.title: Poulenc writes a harpsichord concerto for Landowska
edges.claim: [[poulenc]] composed his Concert champêtre for the harpsichordist Wanda Landowska, a friend and colleague from 1923. She gave the first performance with the Orchestre Symphonique de Paris under Pierre Monteux at the Salle Pleyel on 3 May 1929.

edges.title: Francis Jammes’s poems become Lili Boulanger’s song cycle
edges.claim: [[lili-boulanger]]’s song cycle Clairières dans le ciel is set to poems by Francis Jammes. It stands with her three psalms for chorus and orchestra, the diptych D’un soir triste and D’un matin de printemps, and her Prix de Rome cantata Faust et Hélène among the works that made her reputation.

edges.title: Messiaen notates birdsong and writes it into music

works.to: Le merle noir (1952); Réveil des oiseaux (1953)

edges.claim: [[messiaen]] was fascinated by birdsong and notated it around the world. Birds had appeared in several earlier works, but the flute piece Le merle noir was based entirely on the song of the blackbird; the orchestral Réveil des oiseaux (1953) took the idea further, its material consisting almost entirely of the birdsong one might hear between midnight and noon in the Jura. From then on he incorporated birdsong transcriptions into his compositions.

edges.title: A gift of Pelléas becomes “a thunderbolt” for Messiaen
edges.claim: At Nantes, one of Messiaen’s teachers, Jehan de Gibon, gave him a score of [[debussy]]’s opera Pelléas et Mélisande. [[messiaen]] called it “a thunderbolt” and “probably the most decisive influence on me”. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1919, aged eleven.

edges.title: Ligeti discovers Nancarrow’s player-piano Studies

works.to: Ligeti’s Piano Études and Piano Concerto (1980s)

edges.claim: [[ligeti]] first met Nancarrow’s name through a Berlin festival of mechanical music in January 1980, and was fascinated by the complexity and temporal layering of a score page of Study No. 36 in its catalogue. He called Nancarrow’s music “the greatest discovery since Webern and Ives”. His Piano Études draw on sources that include gamelan, African polyrhythms, Bartók, Monk, Bill Evans and Nancarrow.

sources.title: Nancarrow und Ligeti (nancarrow.de, in German)
sources.locator: the Berlin festival, January 1980; Study No. 36

edges.title: Boulez joins Messiaen’s advanced harmony class

works.from: Messiaen’s private seminars and Conservatoire class

edges.claim: In June 1944 [[boulez]] approached [[messiaen]] and asked to study harmony with him. Messiaen invited him to attend the private seminars he gave to selected students, and in January 1945 Boulez joined his advanced harmony class at the Conservatoire de Paris. He also studied counterpoint privately with Andrée Vaurabourg and, with René Leibowitz, twelve-note technique.

edges.title: Boulez declares “Schoenberg is Dead”
edges.claim: A 1952 article in the British journal The Score, published shortly after [[schoenberg]]’s death, first brought [[boulez]] international attention as a writer. In it he attacked Schoenberg for conservatism, contrasting him with the radicalism of Webern. The article caused widespread controversy, although Boulez had learned twelve-note technique privately with René Leibowitz, a champion of Schoenberg.

edges.title: Boulez folds Mallarmé’s sonnets into Pli selon pli

works.to: Pli selon pli, “Portrait de Mallarmé” (first performed 1960)

edges.claim: [[boulez]]’s Pli selon pli (“Fold by fold”), subtitled Portrait de Mallarmé, is a work in five movements for solo soprano and orchestra whose text is drawn from sonnets by Mallarmé. It was first performed in 1960 at Baden-Baden, sixty-six years after [[debussy]] answered another Mallarmé poem with the Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune.

edges.title: Cage opens publishers’ doors to Boulez

works.from: Sonatas and Interludes for prepared piano (1946–48)

edges.claim: [[boulez]]’s friendship with John Cage began in 1949, when Cage was visiting Paris. Cage introduced him to two publishers, Heugel and Amphion, who agreed to take his recent pieces, and Boulez helped arrange a private performance of Cage’s Sonatas and Interludes for prepared piano.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pierre Boulez
sources.locator: Early career: John Cage and Karlheinz Stockhausen

edges.title: Feldman meets Cage after Webern’s Symphony

works.from: Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21 at Carnegie Hall (January 1950)

edges.claim: In January 1950 [[feldman]] met John Cage walking out of Carnegie Hall, where both had gone to hear the New York Philharmonic under Dimitri Mitropoulos play Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21. Feldman soon moved into Cage’s apartment building on Grand Street, and through Cage met Jackson Pollock, Philip Guston and Frank O’Hara.

edges.title: Rothko’s paintings inspire Feldman’s Rothko Chapel

works.from: Mark Rothko’s paintings in the Rothko Chapel, Houston

edges.claim: In the 1970s [[feldman]] wrote a number of pieces about twenty minutes long, among them Rothko Chapel (1971), written for the building in Houston that houses paintings by Mark Rothko. He found inspiration in abstract expressionist painting and knew its painters through Cage, who introduced him to Jackson Pollock, Philip Guston and Frank O’Hara.

edges.title: Pärt studies chant and Notre Dame polyphony before tintinnabuli

works.from: Gregorian chant and the Notre Dame School
works.to: Für Alina (1976) and the tintinnabuli style

edges.claim: After Credo (1968), [[part]] entered a creative crisis that lasted eight years. During that time he joined the Orthodox Church and studied Gregorian chant, the Notre Dame School and classic vocal polyphony. In 1976 he emerged with a new and highly original musical language that he called tintinnabuli, first heard in the piano piece Für Alina.

sources.title: Arvo Pärt Centre: Arvo Pärt
sources.locator: the crisis and the years of study

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Arvo Pärt
sources.locator: study of medieval music and Notre Dame organum

edges.title: Pärt mourns Britten in a descending cantus
edges.claim: [[part]] composed Cantus in Memoriam Benjamin Britten for string orchestra and bell as an elegy for [[britten]], who died in December 1976. Pärt greatly admired him, describing in Britten the “unusual purity” that he himself sought as a composer. The work is an early example of Pärt’s tintinnabuli style.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cantus in Memoriam Benjamin Britten

edges.title: Reich studies Ewe drumming in Ghana

works.from: Ewe drumming taught by Gideon Alorwoyie, Legon (June 1970)

edges.claim: In June 1970 [[reich]] travelled to the University of Ghana to study polyrhythmic music for five weeks with the Ewe master drummer Gideon Alorwoyie. From this experience, and from A. M. Jones’s Studies in African Music on the Ewe, he drew inspiration for Drumming (1970–71), which he began composing shortly after his return.

edges.title: Reich studies Balinese gamelan in Seattle and Berkeley

works.from: Gamelan semar pegulingan and gambang, studied in summer 1973 and 1974
works.to: Music for Mallet Instruments, Voices and Organ (1973)

edges.claim: In the summers of 1973 and 1974 [[reich]] studied Balinese gamelan, the semar pegulingan and the gambang, at Seattle and Berkeley. The experience influenced his Music for Mallet Instruments, Voices and Organ (1973); in 1974 he began writing Music for 18 Musicians.

edges.title: Kurtág sets Kafka’s fragments for soprano and violin
edges.claim: [[kurtag]]’s Kafka-Fragmente, Op. 24 (1985–87), for soprano and violin, takes extracts from Kafka’s journals and letters and is broken into forty brief settings organised in four sections. Kurtág was fascinated by the bareness of Kafka’s language, by its sadness and despair, its humour and its depth. The soprano Adrienne Csengery and the violinist András Keller gave the first performance at the Witten Festival of Contemporary Chamber Music in 1987.

sources.title: Berliner Festspiele: György Kurtág, Kafka Fragments

edges.title: Cage’s Silence loosens Adams’s modernist training
edges.claim: [[adams]]’s early work was aligned with modernist music, but he began to disagree with its tenets on reading John Cage’s Silence: Lectures and Writings. Teaching at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, he went on to develop a style of his own.
edges.note: The date is not given in the source; the year 1970 stands for the late 1960s and early 1970s of his training and is approximate.

edges.title: A troubadour’s love from afar becomes Saariaho’s opera
edges.claim: [[saariaho]] became familiar in 1993 with the twelfth-century troubadour Jaufré Rudel, the poet of far-off love (amor de lonh). She did not think herself capable of writing an opera until she saw Peter Sellars’s staging of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise at the 1992 Salzburg Festival. With a libretto by Amin Maalouf, L’Amour de loin (“Love from Afar”) was first performed at the Salzburg Festival on 15 August 2000.

edges.title: Adès re-scores three Couperin harpsichord pieces

works.from: Pièces de clavecin: Les Amusemens, Les Tours de passe-passe, L’Âme-en-peine

edges.claim: [[ades]]’s Three Studies from Couperin (2006), written for the Basle Chamber Orchestra, reconfigure keyboard pieces by [[couperin]] — Les Amusemens, Les Tours de passe-passe and L’Âme-en-peine — for two string ensembles with solo winds and percussion. Because Couperin’s style involves a great deal of repetition, Adès varies it by altering the orchestration or adding shadows and haloes to the parts.

sources.title: IRCAM Brahms database: Thomas Adès, Three Studies from Couperin

edges.title: Reger builds an organ monument on BACH

works.to: Fantasie und Fuge über B-A-C-H, Op. 46 (1900)

edges.claim: Reger made B–A–C–H the named subject of his large organ Fantasy and Fugue, Op. 46, composed in February 1900. Its dedication is to Josef Rheinberger: the Bach homage in its musical material should not be confused with the person named on the dedication page.

sources.title: Reger, Fantasie und Fuge über B-A-C-H, Op. 46: work catalogue
sources.locator: General Information: February 1900, organ, dedication to Josef Rheinberger

edges.title: Bach’s four notes begin Webern’s twelve-tone row
edges.claim: Webern’s Op. 28 row begins B♭–A–C–B♮, and its three four-note groups are transformations of that same B–A–C–H cell. The quartet therefore carries an identifiable Bach signature inside its twelve-tone organisation rather than quoting a whole Bach tune.
edges.note: 1938 anchors the completed quartet’s first performance, on 22 September at the Coolidge Festival in Pittsfield, not the start of composition.

sources.title: String Quartet, Op. 28 (Webern): tone-row analysis
sources.locator: ‘Tone row’: opening B-flat–A–C–B-natural and three related tetrachords; opening chronology

sources.title: Universal Edition: Webern, String Quartet Op. 28

edges.title: Pärt places Bach beside twelve-tone dissonance

works.from: The B–A–C–H signature; English Suite in D minor, Sarabande

edges.claim: Pärt’s Collage über B-A-C-H begins its ten-note sequence with Bach’s four-note signature. In the Sarabande, passages from the D-minor English Suite alternate with dense clusters, and harpsichord and piano help distinguish inherited Baroque music from the modern material set against it.

sources.title: Arvo Pärt Centre: Collage über B-A-C-H
sources.locator: 1964 work entry and commentary: ten-note sequence, Sarabande quotation, harpsichord/piano contrast

edges.title: The chant haunts an amplified string quartet

works.to: Black Angels, Thirteen Images from the Dark Land (1970)

edges.claim: Crumb acknowledged the Dies irae among the musical allusions in Black Angels, alongside Schubert’s Death and the Maiden and Tartini’s Devil’s Trill. The chant’s appearance in a work for amplified string quartet extends its afterlife beyond Romantic orchestral spectacle into an intimate, unsettling modern sound-world.

sources.title: Victoria Adamenko, Library of Congress National Recording Registry: Black Angels
sources.locator: p. 2: Crumb’s foreword acknowledges Dies irae and other allusions; pp. 1–2: scoring and 13 March 1970 completion

edges.title: The Ode becomes an anthem without words

works.from: Symphony No. 9, finale, Ode to Joy
works.to: European anthem: Council of Europe adoption (1972), European Community adoption (1985)

edges.claim: The Council of Europe adopted Beethoven’s Ode to Joy melody as its anthem in 1972; European Community leaders adopted it in 1985. The official anthem has no words, allowing the music to serve as a shared symbol without choosing one language for Schiller’s poem.

sources.title: European Union: European anthem
sources.locator: Official page, updated 17 April 2026: 1972 and 1985 adoptions; instrumental anthem without words

edges.title: Bernstein changes joy to freedom in Berlin

works.from: Symphony No. 9, finale, Schiller’s An die Freude

edges.claim: At the Christmas Day 1989 concert in East Berlin, Bernstein conducted Beethoven’s Ninth with singers substituting Freiheit for Freude in the finale. The alteration answered the opening of the Berlin Wall; it is a documented performance decision, not evidence that Schiller originally wrote the poem with that word.

sources.title: Leonard Bernstein Office: Berlin Wall Concert, 1989
sources.locator: Klaus Geitel’s account: 25 December 1989, East Berlin Schauspielhaus, Freude changed to Freiheit

edges.title: A children’s round enters Paperback Writer
edges.claim: The Beatles sing Frère Jacques in the backing vocals of Paperback Writer, recorded in April 1966. Unlike Mahler’s minor-key funeral transformation, this is a brief vocal quotation tucked into a pop recording: the same familiar round travels into a different musical setting.
